title: compare the number of atoms of one element across samples given as a mass, an amount in moles, and a particle count.
stem:
Four samples are described. Molar masses (g/mol): H₂O 18.02, CO₂ 44.01.
Sample 1: 20.0 g of H₂O.
Sample 2: 0.100 mol of Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
Sample 3: 30.0 g of CO₂.
Sample 4: 2.40 × 10²³ molecules of SO₃.
Which sample contains the greatest number of oxygen atoms? (Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample 3, which contains about 1.36 mol of oxygen atoms.
choices.rationale: Correct: Convert each to mol of O atoms: 1.11, 0.800, 2 × (30.0/44.01) = 1.36, and 3 × (2.40 × 10²³/6.022 × 10²³) = 1.20; the largest is sample 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample 1, because it has the largest amount of substance (1.11 mol) of the four.
choices.rationale: Sample 1 has the most moles of molecules, but each H₂O has only one O atom, so it holds 1.11 mol of O atoms, fewer than sample 3 at 1.36 mol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample 2, because each formula unit of Ca₃(PO₄)₂ contains eight oxygen atoms, more than any other formula.
choices.rationale: Sample 2 has the most O atoms per formula unit, but only 0.100 mol of formula units, giving 0.800 mol of O atoms, the fewest of the four.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample 4, because a count of 2.40 × 10²³ is a number of particles and therefore the largest quantity listed.
choices.rationale: Sample 4 is 0.399 mol of SO₃ with three O atoms each, which is 1.20 mol of O atoms; this is large but still less than sample 3 at 1.36 mol.

title: compare the number of atoms of one element across samples given as a mass, an amount in moles, and a particle count. (variant 1)
stem:
Four samples are described. Molar masses (g/mol): NH₃ 17.03.
Sample 1: 15.0 g of NH₃.
Sample 2: 0.800 mol of C₂H₅OH.
Sample 3: 0.300 mol of C₆H₁₂O₆.
Sample 4: 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules of H₂SO₄.
Which sample contains the greatest number of hydrogen atoms? (Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample 2, which contains 4.80 mol of hydrogen atoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample 1, because ammonia has the lowest molar mass, so 15.0 g contains the most molecules.
choices.rationale: The 15.0 g of NH₃ is 0.881 mol of molecules, but at three H atoms each it gives only 2.64 mol of H atoms, less than sample 2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample 3, because glucose has twelve hydrogen atoms per molecule, more than any other formula.
choices.rationale: Glucose has the most H per molecule, but 0.300 mol gives only 3.60 mol of H atoms, which is less than the 4.80 mol in sample 2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample 4, because it is stated as a count of particles and 1.20 × 10²⁴ is the largest number.
choices.rationale: The 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules are 1.99 mol of H₂SO₄ with two H each, so 3.99 mol of H atoms; this is below sample 2 at 4.80 mol.

title: compare the number of atoms of one element across samples given as a mass, an amount in moles, and a particle count. (variant 2)
stem:
Four samples are described. Molar masses (g/mol): CCl₄ 153.82, AlCl₃ 133.34.
Sample 1: 40.0 g of CCl₄.
Sample 2: 0.500 mol of MgCl₂.
Sample 3: 60.0 g of AlCl₃.
Sample 4: 2.00 × 10²³ molecules of PCl₃.
Which sample contains the greatest number of chlorine atoms? (Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample 1, because CCl₄ has four chlorine atoms per molecule, the most of any formula listed.
choices.rationale: Four Cl per molecule is the most, but 40.0 g is only 0.260 mol of CCl₄, giving 1.04 mol of Cl atoms, less than the 1.35 mol in sample 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample 2, because it is the only sample stated directly in moles, so no conversion is needed to compare it.
choices.rationale: Sample 2 gives 0.500 mol × 2 = 1.00 mol of Cl atoms; the way a quantity is stated does not make it larger, and sample 3 holds 1.35 mol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample 4, because each PCl₃ molecule contains three chlorine atoms and phosphorus is heavier than aluminum.
choices.rationale: Sample 4 is 0.332 mol of PCl₃, giving only 0.996 mol of Cl atoms; the mass of the other element does not affect the count of Cl atoms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample 3, which contains about 1.35 mol of chlorine atoms.

title: compare the number of atoms of one element across samples given as a mass, an amount in moles, and a particle count. (variant 3)
stem:
Four samples are described. Molar masses (g/mol): NH₃ 17.03, NaNO₃ 84.99.
Sample 1: 25.0 g of NH₃.
Sample 2: 0.600 mol of NH₄NO₃.
Sample 3: 50.0 g of NaNO₃.
Sample 4: 4.00 × 10²³ molecules of N₂O₄.
Which sample contains the greatest number of nitrogen atoms? (Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample 2, because NH₄NO₃ contains two nitrogen atoms per formula unit and its amount is given directly in moles.
choices.rationale: The 0.600 mol of NH₄NO₃ gives 1.20 mol of N atoms; two N per formula unit does not offset the smaller number of formula units compared with sample 1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample 3, because the 50.0 g is the largest mass of any compound that contains nitrogen.
choices.rationale: Sample 3 is 0.588 mol of NaNO₃ with one N atom each, so 0.588 mol of N atoms; a large mass does not mean many atoms when the molar mass is large.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample 4, because N₂O₄ has two nitrogen atoms per molecule and a particle count of the order 10²³.
choices.rationale: Sample 4 is 0.664 mol of N₂O₄, giving 1.33 mol of N atoms, which is close to but smaller than the 1.47 mol in sample 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample 1, which contains about 1.47 mol of nitrogen atoms.

title: identify an unknown element from the number of atoms of another element in a mass of its compound, using the formula to
stem: A 5.00 g sample of an unknown alkali-metal carbonate, M₂CO₃, contains 6.54 × 10²² oxygen atoms. Use the molar masses (g/mol) C 12.01, O 16.00, S 32.06, N 14.01, P 30.97, Li 6.94, Na 22.99, K 39.10, Rb 85.47, Mg 24.31, Ca 40.08, Sr 87.62, Ba 137.33. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. What is M?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Li, because lithium is the lightest alkali metal and the sample is small.
choices.rationale: Li₂CO₃ (73.89 g/mol) would give 5.00/73.89 × 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.22 × 10²³ O atoms, nearly twice the value observed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Na, because Na₂CO₃ is the most common carbonate and its formula contains three oxygen atoms.
choices.rationale: Na₂CO₃ (105.99 g/mol) would give 8.52 × 10²² O atoms in 5.00 g, which is more than the 6.54 × 10²² observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rb, because the sample must contain more than one mole of metal atoms to account for 10²² oxygen atoms.
choices.rationale: Rb₂CO₃ (230.94 g/mol) would give only 3.91 × 10²² O atoms in 5.00 g; also 10²² atoms is far less than one mole, so no such requirement exists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K, because 6.54 × 10²² O atoms is 0.109 mol of O, so 0.0362 mol of M₂CO₃, a molar mass of 138 g/mol.

title: identify an unknown element from the number of atoms of another element in a mass of its compound, using the formula to  (variant 1)
stem: A 6.00 g sample of an unknown alkali-metal sulfate, M₂SO₄, contains 1.02 × 10²³ oxygen atoms. Use the molar masses (g/mol) C 12.01, O 16.00, S 32.06, N 14.01, P 30.97, Li 6.94, Na 22.99, K 39.10, Rb 85.47, Mg 24.31, Ca 40.08, Sr 87.62, Ba 137.33. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. What is M?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Li, because a lighter metal gives a smaller molar mass and therefore more oxygen atoms per gram.
choices.rationale: Li₂SO₄ (109.94 g/mol) would give 1.31 × 10²³ O atoms in 6.00 g, which is more than the 1.02 × 10²³ observed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: K, because K₂SO₄ is the sulfate most often used as a standard and contains four oxygen atoms per formula unit.
choices.rationale: K₂SO₄ (174.26 g/mol) would give 8.29 × 10²² O atoms in 6.00 g, which is less than the 1.02 × 10²³ observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rb, because a count of 10²³ atoms of oxygen is too large to come from a light metal.
choices.rationale: Rb₂SO₄ (267.00 g/mol) would give only 5.41 × 10²² O atoms in 6.00 g; the number of oxygen atoms depends on the molar mass of the whole formula unit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Na, because the O count gives 0.0423 mol of M₂SO₄, a molar mass of 142 g/mol, so M = 22.99.
choices.rationale: Correct: 1.02 × 10²³/6.022 × 10²³ = 0.1694 mol O; ÷ 4 = 0.04235 mol; 6.00/0.04235 = 141.7 g/mol; minus 96.06 for SO₄ gives 45.6 for 2 M, so M = 22.8, sodium.

title: identify an unknown element from the number of atoms of another element in a mass of its compound, using the formula to  (variant 2)
stem: A 8.00 g sample of an unknown alkaline-earth nitrate, M(NO₃)₂, contains 4.55 × 10²² nitrogen atoms. Use the molar masses (g/mol) C 12.01, O 16.00, S 32.06, N 14.01, P 30.97, Li 6.94, Na 22.99, K 39.10, Rb 85.47, Mg 24.31, Ca 40.08, Sr 87.62, Ba 137.33. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. What is M?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mg, because Mg(NO₃)₂ has the smallest formula mass, so the sample holds the fewest atoms.
choices.rationale: Mg(NO₃)₂ (148.31 g/mol) would give 8.00/148.31 × 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.50 × 10²² N atoms, more than observed; a smaller formula mass gives more atoms, not fewer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ca, because Ca(NO₃)₂ is the nitrate whose count of N atoms is closest to 5 × 10²².
choices.rationale: Ca(NO₃)₂ (164.10 g/mol) would give 5.87 × 10²² N atoms in 8.00 g, which does not match the 4.55 × 10²² observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sr, because 4.55 × 10²² N atoms is 0.0378 mol of M(NO₃)₂, a molar mass of 212 g/mol.
choices.rationale: Correct: 4.55 × 10²²/6.022 × 10²³ = 0.07556 mol N; ÷ 2 = 0.03778 mol; 8.00/0.03778 = 211.8 g/mol; minus 124.02 for 2 NO₃ gives 87.7, strontium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ba, because dividing the N atoms by two formula units gives a metal mass near 137 g/mol.
choices.rationale: Ba(NO₃)₂ (261.35 g/mol) would give 3.69 × 10²² N atoms in 8.00 g; the factor of two relates N atoms to formula units, not to the molar mass of the metal.

title: identify an unknown element from the number of atoms of another element in a mass of its compound, using the formula to  (variant 3)
stem: A 4.00 g sample of an unknown alkali-metal phosphate, M₃PO₄, contains 4.54 × 10²² oxygen atoms. Use the molar masses (g/mol) C 12.01, O 16.00, S 32.06, N 14.01, P 30.97, Li 6.94, Na 22.99, K 39.10, Rb 85.47, Mg 24.31, Ca 40.08, Sr 87.62, Ba 137.33. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. What is M?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Li, because Li₃PO₄ has the smallest formula mass and four oxygen atoms per formula unit.
choices.rationale: Li₃PO₄ (115.79 g/mol) would give 4.00/115.79 × 4 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 8.32 × 10²² O atoms, almost twice the observed number.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Na, because Na₃PO₄ is a common phosphate and three metal atoms balance one phosphate ion.
choices.rationale: Na₃PO₄ (163.94 g/mol) would give 5.88 × 10²² O atoms in 4.00 g, which is more than the 4.54 × 10²² observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: K, because the O count gives 0.0188 mol of M₃PO₄, a molar mass of 212 g/mol, so M = 39.1.
choices.rationale: Correct: 4.54 × 10²²/6.022 × 10²³ = 0.07539 mol O; ÷ 4 = 0.01885 mol; 4.00/0.01885 = 212.2 g/mol; minus 94.97 for PO₄ gives 117.2 for 3 M, so M = 39.1, potassium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rb, because the unknown metal must be heavy to account for the small number of oxygen atoms.
choices.rationale: Rb₃PO₄ (351.38 g/mol) would give only 2.74 × 10²² O atoms in 4.00 g, fewer than observed.

title: interpret the molecular-ion peaks of a diatomic element, where each element's isotope abundances must be recovered from
stem: The mass spectrum of a sample of chlorine gas, Cl₂, shows three peaks from singly charged Cl₂⁺ ions: m/z 70 (relative height 9), m/z 72 (relative height 6) and m/z 74 (relative height 1). The only isotopes are ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Treat isotope masses as equal to their mass numbers. What is the average atomic mass of chlorine in this sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 35.5, because the 70 : 72 : 74 heights of 9 : 6 : 1 correspond to 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl.
choices.rationale: Correct: p² = 9/16 so the fraction of ³⁵Cl is 0.75 and of ³⁷Cl is 0.25 (check: 2pq = 6/16); average = 35(0.75) + 37(0.25) = 35.5.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 71.0, because it is the weighted average of the three peak positions.
choices.rationale: The weighted average of the peaks is 71.0, but that is the average mass of a Cl₂ molecule; the atomic mass is half of it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 36.0, because the average of the two isotope masses, 35 and 37, is 36.
choices.rationale: A simple average of 35 and 37 ignores abundance; the 9 : 6 : 1 pattern shows ³⁵Cl is far more abundant, so the average must be closer to 35.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 35.0, because the tallest peak at m/z 70 corresponds to the most abundant isotope.
choices.rationale: The tallest peak is ³⁵Cl₂, but 25% of the atoms are ³⁷Cl, which raises the average above 35.

title: interpret the molecular-ion peaks of a diatomic element, where each element's isotope abundances must be recovered from  (variant 1)
stem: The mass spectrum of a sample of bromine, Br₂, shows peaks from singly charged Br₂⁺ ions at m/z 158, 160 and 162 with relative heights 1 : 2 : 1. The only isotopes are ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br. Treat isotope masses as equal to their mass numbers. What is the average atomic mass of bromine in this sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 160.0, because it is the position of the tallest peak in the spectrum.
choices.rationale: The tallest peak at 160 is the mass of a Br₂ molecule; the atomic mass is half, so 80.0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 79.0, because ⁷⁹Br is the lighter isotope and gives the first peak.
choices.rationale: The first peak at 158 is ⁷⁹Br₂, but equal numbers of ⁸¹Br atoms are present, so the average is not the lighter isotope mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 80.0, because the 1 : 2 : 1 pattern shows the two isotopes are equally abundant.
choices.rationale: Correct: p² = 1/4 gives p = 0.50 for each isotope (2pq = 1/2 matches the middle peak); average = 79(0.50) + 81(0.50) = 80.0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 81.0, because the heaviest peak at m/z 162 corresponds to the heaviest isotope, which sets the atomic mass.
choices.rationale: The heaviest peak shows that ⁸¹Br exists, but it is only one of the two equally abundant isotopes, so the average is not 81.

title: interpret the molecular-ion peaks of a diatomic element, where each element's isotope abundances must be recovered from  (variant 2)
stem: A sample of chlorine gas enriched in the heavier isotope gives a mass spectrum with peaks from Cl₂⁺ ions at m/z 70, 72 and 74 with relative heights 1 : 4 : 4. The only isotopes are ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Treat isotope masses as equal to their mass numbers. What is the average atomic mass of chlorine in this sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 72.7, because it is the average mass of the Cl₂ molecules.
choices.rationale: The weighted average of the peak positions is 72.7, but this is the mass of a Cl₂ molecule; the atomic mass is half of it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 36.0, because the two tallest peaks are equal, so the isotopes are equally abundant.
choices.rationale: The tallest two peaks have equal height, but the peak at 72 counts one atom of each isotope while 74 counts two ³⁷Cl, so ³⁷Cl is more abundant than ³⁵Cl.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 35.0, because the lightest peak at m/z 70 is the base for the average.
choices.rationale: The 70 peak is only ³⁵Cl₂, the smallest peak here; the isotope with mass 37 is the most abundant, so the average is above 36.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 36.3, because ³⁷Cl accounts for two thirds of the atoms.
choices.rationale: Correct: q² = 4/9 for ³⁷Cl₂ gives ³⁷Cl = 2/3 of the atoms (2pq = 4/9 checks); average = 35(1/3) + 37(2/3) = 36.3.

title: interpret the molecular-ion peaks of a diatomic element, where each element's isotope abundances must be recovered from  (variant 3)
stem: A sample of bromine gas that is depleted in ⁸¹Br gives a mass spectrum with peaks from Br₂⁺ ions at m/z 158, 160 and 162 with relative heights 16 : 8 : 1. The only isotopes are ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br. Treat isotope masses as equal to their mass numbers. What is the average atomic mass of bromine in this sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 158.8, because it is the weighted average mass of a Br₂ molecule.
choices.rationale: The weighted average of the peaks is 158.8, but this is for a Br₂ molecule; the atomic mass is half, 79.4.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 79.4, because ⁷⁹Br makes up 80% of the atoms and ⁸¹Br makes up 20%.
choices.rationale: Correct: p² = 16/25 so the fraction of ⁷⁹Br is 0.80 (2pq = 8/25 checks); average = 79(0.80) + 81(0.20) = 79.4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 80.0, because the mean of the isotope masses 79 and 81 is the atomic mass.
choices.rationale: The unweighted mean of 79 and 81 ignores that ⁷⁹Br is four times as abundant as ⁸¹Br in this sample.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 79.0, because the tallest peak at m/z 158 shows that ⁷⁹Br is the only significant isotope.
choices.rationale: The tallest peak shows ⁷⁹Br dominates, but the 20% ⁸¹Br raises the average above 79.

title: use both the m/z values and the isotope pattern (peak spacing and relative heights) in a mass spectrum to decide how man
stem: A pure compound that contains only carbon, hydrogen and one type of halogen gives a mass spectrum with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 112 (relative height 100) and m/z 114 (relative height 32), and no other peaks in that region. Use the isotope masses ¹²C = 12, ¹H = 1, ³⁵Cl = 35, ³⁷Cl = 37, ⁷⁹Br = 79 and ⁸¹Br = 81, and ignore ¹³C and ²H. Natural chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl; natural bromine is about 51% ⁷⁹Br and 49% ⁸¹Br. Which formula is consistent with the spectrum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C₈H₁₆, because a hydrocarbon with 8 carbons and 16 hydrogens also has a mass of 112.
choices.rationale: C₈H₁₆ has mass 112 but contains no halogen, so it would give a single peak with no peak at 114 of height 32.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C₆H₅Cl, because its mass is 112 and the 3 : 1 pair separated by two mass units is the signature of one chlorine atom.
choices.rationale: Correct: C₆H₅³⁵Cl = 72 + 5 + 35 = 112 and C₆H₅³⁷Cl = 114; the 100 : 32 ratio is about 75 : 25 for ³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl, so one Cl atom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: C₃H₆Cl₂, because it also has a mass of 112 and contains chlorine.
choices.rationale: C₃H₆Cl₂ has mass 112 but two Cl atoms would give peaks at 112, 114 and 116 in a 9 : 6 : 1 ratio, so the 114 peak would be about 2/3 of the base peak, not 32%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: C₆H₅Br, because any halogen produces a peak two mass units above the molecular ion.
choices.rationale: C₆H₅Br would have its molecular ions at m/z 156 and 158 in a 1 : 1 ratio, not at 112 and 114 in a 3 : 1 ratio.

title: use both the m/z values and the isotope pattern (peak spacing and relative heights) in a mass spectrum to decide how man (variant 1)
stem: A pure compound that contains only carbon, hydrogen and one type of halogen gives a mass spectrum with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 94 and m/z 96 of nearly equal height (100 and 98), and no other peaks in that region. Use the isotope masses ¹²C = 12, ¹H = 1, ³⁵Cl = 35, ³⁷Cl = 37, ⁷⁹Br = 79 and ⁸¹Br = 81, and ignore ¹³C and ²H. Natural chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl; natural bromine is about 51% ⁷⁹Br and 49% ⁸¹Br. Which formula is consistent with the spectrum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C₇H₁₀, because a hydrocarbon of this formula also has a mass of 94.
choices.rationale: C₇H₁₀ has mass 94 but contains no halogen, so it would give one peak at 94 and no peak at 96 of comparable height.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CH₃Cl, because chlorine also gives a pair of peaks separated by two mass units.
choices.rationale: CH₃Cl would give peaks at m/z 50 and 52 in a 3 : 1 ratio; neither the masses nor the ratio match the spectrum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CH₃Br, because its mass is 94 and a 1 : 1 pair two mass units apart is the signature of one bromine atom.
choices.rationale: Correct: CH₃⁷⁹Br = 12 + 3 + 79 = 94 and CH₃⁸¹Br = 96; two equal peaks two units apart indicate one Br atom, since ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are almost equally abundant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CH₂Br₂, because two peaks of equal height imply two bromine atoms.
choices.rationale: CH₂Br₂ would give three peaks at 172, 174 and 176 in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio; one atom of bromine gives two equal peaks.

title: use both the m/z values and the isotope pattern (peak spacing and relative heights) in a mass spectrum to decide how man (variant 2)
stem: A pure compound that contains only carbon, hydrogen and chlorine gives a mass spectrum with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 118, 120, 122 and 124 with relative heights 100, 96, 31 and 3. Use the isotope masses ¹²C = 12, ¹H = 1, ³⁵Cl = 35, ³⁷Cl = 37, ⁷⁹Br = 79 and ⁸¹Br = 81, and ignore ¹³C and ²H. Natural chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl; natural bromine is about 51% ⁷⁹Br and 49% ⁸¹Br. Which formula is consistent with the spectrum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C₉H₁₀, because a hydrocarbon of this formula has a mass of 118.
choices.rationale: C₉H₁₀ has mass 118 but contains no chlorine, so it would show one peak and not four peaks spaced two mass units apart.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CH₂Cl₂, because the pattern of several peaks shows that chlorine is present.
choices.rationale: CH₂Cl₂ would have molecular ions at 84, 86 and 88 in a 9 : 6 : 1 ratio, so it gives three peaks at lower mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CHBr₃, because four peaks are produced by a compound with three halogen atoms.
choices.rationale: CHBr₃ also has three halogen atoms but its peaks would be near m/z 250 to 256, and the ratio would be about 1 : 3 : 3 : 1, not 100 : 96 : 31 : 3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CHCl₃, because its mass is 118 and four peaks in a ratio near 27 : 27 : 9 : 1 indicate three chlorine atoms.
choices.rationale: Correct: CH³⁵Cl₃ = 12 + 1 + 105 = 118; the binomial pattern (0.75 + 0.25)³ = 0.42 : 0.42 : 0.14 : 0.016 matches 100 : 96 : 31 : 3 for three Cl atoms.

title: use both the m/z values and the isotope pattern (peak spacing and relative heights) in a mass spectrum to decide how man (variant 3)
stem: A pure compound that contains only carbon, hydrogen and bromine gives a mass spectrum with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 172 (relative height 50), 174 (100) and 176 (49). Use the isotope masses ¹²C = 12, ¹H = 1, ³⁵Cl = 35, ³⁷Cl = 37, ⁷⁹Br = 79 and ⁸¹Br = 81, and ignore ¹³C and ²H. Natural chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl; natural bromine is about 51% ⁷⁹Br and 49% ⁸¹Br. Which formula is consistent with the spectrum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CH₂Br₂, because its mass is 172 and the 1 : 2 : 1 pattern of three peaks indicates two bromine atoms.
choices.rationale: Correct: CH₂⁷⁹Br₂ = 12 + 2 + 158 = 172, with ⁷⁹Br⁸¹Br at 174 and ⁸¹Br₂ at 176; (0.5 + 0.5)² gives 1 : 2 : 1 for two Br atoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C₁₃H₁₆, because a hydrocarbon of this formula also has a mass of 172.
choices.rationale: C₁₃H₁₆ has mass 172 but contains no bromine, so it would show a single molecular-ion peak instead of three peaks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CH₂Cl₂, because three peaks with a ratio near 1 : 2 : 1 are produced by two chlorine atoms.
choices.rationale: CH₂Cl₂ is two halogen atoms, but chlorine gives a 9 : 6 : 1 ratio and the peaks would be at 84, 86 and 88.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CHBr₃, because the three peaks show that the molecule contains three bromine atoms.
choices.rationale: CHBr₃ would give four peaks near m/z 250 in a ratio of about 1 : 3 : 3 : 1; the number of peaks is one more than the number of Br atoms, so three peaks mean two Br atoms.

choices.label: A
choices.text: C₃H₆O₃, because the empirical formula is CH₂O (30.03 g/mol) and 90.1 divided by 30.03 is 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CH₂O, because that is the simplest whole-number ratio of C, H and O.

choices.label: C

title: explain why a measured empirical formula deviates from the expected one, using the mass change on forming a nitride vers
stem: A student heats 0.486 g of magnesium ribbon strongly in an open crucible until it stops glowing, then weighs the product: 0.790 g. Assuming all of the mass gained is oxygen, the student calculates 0.304 g of O (0.0190 mol) combined with 0.0200 mol of Mg, a Mg : O mole ratio of 1.05 : 1 instead of 1 : 1. When a little water is added to the cooled white product, a gas with an ammonia odor is released and no gray metal remains. Which explanation is most consistent with all of the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some magnesium did not react and remained as metal, so the product mass is too small.
choices.rationale: Unreacted Mg would also lower the mass gain, but the observation of no gray metal rules it out and it would not release an ammonia-smelling gas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The product absorbed water vapor from the air, which added mass and made the apparent oxygen too high.
choices.rationale: Extra mass from water would increase the calculated O and give a Mg : O ratio below 1 : 1, the opposite of the 1.05 : 1 found.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some of the magnesium reacted with N₂ to form Mg₃N₂, which gains less mass per mole of Mg than MgO, so the calculated O is too low.
choices.rationale: Correct: Mg₃N₂ adds 14.01 × 2/3 = 9.3 g per mole of Mg versus 16.00 g for MgO, so a mixed product weighs less than MgO (0.806 g expected); water on a nitride gives NH₃.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some magnesium formed MgO₂, a peroxide, which adds more oxygen per mole of Mg than MgO.
choices.rationale: A peroxide would add extra oxygen and give a Mg : O ratio below 1 : 1; it also would not release ammonia on adding water.

title: use successive ionization energies and Coulomb's law to explain how electron-electron shielding within the same shell ch
stem: The energy needed to remove one electron from a species in the gas phase is listed in kJ/mol: H, 1312; He, 2372; He⁺, 5250. Each removal is of a 1s electron. Which statement best accounts for all three values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 1s electron in He is attracted by a +2 nucleus but is partly shielded by the other 1s electron, so it is held less strongly than the unshielded 1s electron in He⁺.
choices.rationale: Correct: H, He and He⁺ all lose a 1s electron; He⁺ has no second electron to repel and feels the full +2, so 5250 > 2372, while He feels less than +2 but more than +1, so 1312 < 2372.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 1s electron in He is at a higher energy level than in H, so less energy is needed to remove it.
choices.rationale: Both electrons are in the n = 1 shell; the larger value for He than for H shows the nuclear charge matters, so level is not the reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nuclear charge of He⁺ is larger than that of He because the ion has lost an electron.
choices.rationale: The nuclear charge is +2 in both He and He⁺; only the number of electrons differs, and the electron-electron repulsion is what changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second 1s electron in He shields the first completely, so the energy to remove it would be the same as for H.
choices.rationale: Complete shielding would make He the same as H, but the value for He is much larger than for H; the shielding is only partial.

title: use successive ionization energies and Coulomb's law to explain how electron-electron shielding within the same shell ch (variant 1)
stem: The energy needed to remove a 1s electron from lithium species in the gas phase is: Li⁺ → Li²⁺, 7298 kJ/mol; Li²⁺ → Li³⁺, 11815 kJ/mol. Why does the second removal require so much more energy than the first, although both are 1s electrons in the same nucleus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Li⁺ the two 1s electrons shield each other, so each feels less than +3; in Li²⁺ the lone 1s electron feels the full +3 charge.
choices.rationale: Correct: Both are 1s electrons with the same +3 nucleus; electron-electron repulsion in Li⁺ partially offsets the attraction, so IE₂ < IE₃.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The remaining electron in Li²⁺ is in a lower energy level than the electron removed from Li⁺.
choices.rationale: Both electrons occupy the n = 1 level; the energy gap is not due to a change in level.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nucleus of Li²⁺ has a greater charge than the nucleus of Li⁺ because it has lost an electron.
choices.rationale: Removing an electron does not change the number of protons; both species have a +3 nucleus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two 1s electrons in Li⁺ are paired and spin-pairing makes the first electron harder to remove.
choices.rationale: Pairing does not make the first electron harder to remove: the first removal needs less energy (7298), so the second 1s electron, feeling less repulsion, needs more.

title: use successive ionization energies and Coulomb's law to explain how electron-electron shielding within the same shell ch (variant 2)
stem: The energy needed to remove a 1s electron from beryllium species in the gas phase is: Be²⁺ → Be³⁺, 14849 kJ/mol; Be³⁺ → Be⁴⁺, 21007 kJ/mol. Why does the second removal require much more energy than the first, although both are 1s electrons in the same nucleus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 1s electron in Be³⁺ is closer to the nucleus because the nuclear charge of the ion has increased.
choices.rationale: The nuclear charge is +4 in both species; the difference in attraction arises from loss of electron repulsion, not a change in protons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Be²⁺ the two 1s electrons partly shield each other, but in Be³⁺ the one remaining 1s electron feels the full +4 nuclear charge.
choices.rationale: Correct: Both removals are from n = 1 with Z = 4; shielding by the second 1s electron reduces the effective charge in Be²⁺, so 14849 < 21007.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The electron removed from Be²⁺ is in a 2s orbital, which needs less energy than a 1s electron.
choices.rationale: Be²⁺ has the configuration 1s², so both removals are from the 1s orbital; the 2s electrons were removed earlier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Be³⁺ has a smaller radius than Be²⁺, and a smaller radius always doubles the energy required.
choices.rationale: A smaller radius is a consequence of the greater effective charge, not an independent cause, and no rule gives a doubling; the ratio here is 21007/14849 = 1.4.

title: use successive ionization energies and Coulomb's law to explain how electron-electron shielding within the same shell ch (variant 3)
stem: The energy needed to remove a 1s electron from boron species in the gas phase is: B³⁺ → B⁴⁺, 25026 kJ/mol; B⁴⁺ → B⁵⁺, 32827 kJ/mol. Why does the second removal require more energy than the first, although both are 1s electrons in the same nucleus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B⁴⁺ has a larger nuclear charge than B³⁺ because removing an electron exposes more of the nucleus.
choices.rationale: The nucleus has +5 in both ions; exposing the nucleus is not a change in protons, and the effect is due to reduced electron-electron repulsion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In B³⁺ the two 1s electrons partly shield each other, but in B⁴⁺ the one remaining 1s electron feels the full +5 nuclear charge.
choices.rationale: Correct: Both removals are from n = 1 with Z = 5; losing the other 1s electron removes repulsion, so the effective charge rises and 25026 < 32827.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first electron is removed from the 2p subshell and the second from the 1s subshell.
choices.rationale: B³⁺ has only the 1s² electrons left; both ionizations in this question are from the 1s orbital.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electron removed from B⁴⁺ is in a lower shell because the ion is smaller.
choices.rationale: Both electrons are in n = 1; the smaller size of B⁴⁺ is a consequence of the reduced shielding and increased effective charge, not a different shell.

title: predict how peak positions in a photoelectron spectrum change between isoelectronic species, separating the number of el
stem: The photoelectron spectrum of neutral argon has five peaks with relative areas 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6. A different species X gives a spectrum with five peaks in the same 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 ratio, but every peak of X is at a higher binding energy than the corresponding peak of argon. Which species could X be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cl⁻, because it has the same 18 electrons as argon, and the extra electron charge increases the binding.
choices.rationale: Cl⁻ has the same electron count but a nuclear charge of only +17, so its electrons are bound less tightly than argon's and every peak is at lower energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ca, because its electron configuration begins with the same filled subshells as argon.
choices.rationale: Neutral Ca has twenty electrons and would show a sixth peak (4s², area 2), so it does not give five peaks in the 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 ratio.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ar⁺, because removing an electron from argon makes the remaining electrons more tightly bound.
choices.rationale: Ar⁺ has only 17 electrons so the 3p peak would have an area of 5 rather than 6, which does not match the given ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K⁺, because it has the same 18 electrons as argon but a nuclear charge of +19 instead of +18, so every electron is held more tightly.
choices.rationale: Correct: The 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 ratio means 18 electrons in 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p; higher binding energies require a nuclear charge above +18, which fits K⁺ (+19).

title: predict how peak positions in a photoelectron spectrum change between isoelectronic species, separating the number of el (variant 1)
stem: The photoelectron spectrum of neutral neon has three peaks with relative areas 2 : 2 : 6. A different species X gives a spectrum with three peaks in the same 2 : 2 : 6 ratio, but every peak of X is at a higher binding energy than the corresponding peak of neon. Which species could X be?

choices.label: D

choices.rationale: He⁺ has only one electron, so its single peak would have an area of 1 and not 2.

stem: The first five successive ionization energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 and 14842 kJ/mol. Element X forms a compound XClₙ with chlorine in which X uses all of its valence electrons. Which formula and justification are consistent with these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: XCl₄, because the fourth ionization energy is the first very large value, so four electrons must be used.
choices.rationale: The large value of IE₄ shows that the fourth electron comes from an inner shell; the valence electrons are the three removed before the jump.

choices.label: B
choices.text: XCl, because the first ionization energy is the lowest and only one electron is removed easily.
choices.rationale: IE₂ and IE₃ are only 3 to 5 times IE₁, far less than the jump at IE₄, so three electrons are valence, not one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: XCl₅, because five ionization energies are listed and each corresponds to a bond.
choices.rationale: The number of values given is arbitrary; the jump at IE₄ locates the end of the valence shell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: XCl₃, because the large jump occurs between the third and fourth ionization energies, so there are three valence electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: Ratios of successive IE: 3.1, 1.5, 4.2, 1.3; the 4.2 jump (IE₄/IE₃) marks the inner core, so X has three valence electrons.

stem: The first five successive ionization energies of an element X are 496, 4562, 6910, 9543 and 13354 kJ/mol. Element X forms a compound XClₙ with chlorine in which X uses all of its valence electrons. Which formula and justification are consistent with these data?

title: order the radii of isoelectronic ions by using nuclear charge with a fixed electron count, resisting the trends for neut
stem: Consider the ions O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, which all have 10 electrons. Which list gives them in order of decreasing radius, with the correct reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺, because each has the same number of electrons, so the ion with the fewest protons holds them least tightly.
choices.rationale: Correct: All have 1s²2s²2p⁶; the nuclear charges are +8, +9, +11 and +12, so attraction increases and radius decreases from O²⁻ to Mg²⁺.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > O²⁻ > F⁻, because atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period and sodium is at the left.
choices.rationale: This applies the trend for neutral atoms, but these ions all have 10 electrons in n = 2, so nuclear charge alone decides: the cations are smaller than the anions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻, because the ion with the most protons has the most positive charge to hold the electrons far away.
choices.rationale: More protons pull the 10 electrons in more strongly, so Mg²⁺ with +12 is the smallest, not the largest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: O²⁻ > Mg²⁺ > F⁻ > Na⁺, because larger charge magnitude means a larger ion whether positive or negative.
choices.rationale: Radius is not set by charge magnitude; Mg²⁺ with 12 protons holds the 10 electrons more tightly than F⁻ with 9, so Mg²⁺ is smaller than F⁻.

title: order the radii of isoelectronic ions by using nuclear charge with a fixed electron count, resisting the trends for neut (variant 1)
stem: Consider the ions S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺ and Ca²⁺, which all have 18 electrons. Which list gives them in order of decreasing radius, with the correct reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K⁺ > Ca²⁺ > S²⁻ > Cl⁻, because the atoms in period 4 are larger than the atoms in period 3.
choices.rationale: K and Ca atoms are larger than S and Cl atoms, but the ions have identical electron configurations, so the number of protons decides the radius.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ca²⁺ > K⁺ > Cl⁻ > S²⁻, because more protons make the electron cloud larger.
choices.rationale: More protons attract the same 18 electrons more strongly, so Ca²⁺ is the smallest of the four.

choices.label: C
choices.text: S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺, because each has the same number of electrons, so the ion with the fewest protons holds them least tightly.
choices.rationale: Correct: All have 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶; the nuclear charges are +16, +17, +19 and +20, so radius decreases from S²⁻ to Ca²⁺.

choices.label: D
choices.text: S²⁻ > Ca²⁺ > Cl⁻ > K⁺, because radius increases with the magnitude of the charge.
choices.rationale: Charge magnitude does not set the radius; Ca²⁺ has 20 protons holding 18 electrons, so it is smaller than Cl⁻ with 17 protons.

title: order the radii of isoelectronic ions by using nuclear charge with a fixed electron count, resisting the trends for neut (variant 2)
stem: Consider P³⁻, S²⁻, Cl⁻ and Ar, which all have 18 electrons. Which list gives them in order of increasing radius, with the correct reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P³⁻ < S²⁻ < Cl⁻ < Ar, because atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
choices.rationale: This follows the trend for neutral atoms; here all four have 18 electrons, so the one with the fewest protons, P³⁻ (+15), has the largest radius.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ar < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻, because each has the same number of electrons, so the species with the most protons holds them most tightly.
choices.rationale: Correct: All have 18 electrons; nuclear charges are +18 (Ar), +17, +16 and +15, so radius increases Ar < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ar < P³⁻ < S²⁻ < Cl⁻, because a noble gas has a complete outer shell and so is the smallest and the more negative the ion the larger.
choices.rationale: The first part is right but the order of the anions is wrong: with 18 electrons, the ion with the fewest protons is largest, so P³⁻ is the largest, not Cl⁻.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻ < Ar, because neutral atoms have extra electron repulsion that makes them largest.
choices.rationale: Ar has the highest nuclear charge (+18) of the four holding the same 18 electrons, so it is the smallest, not the largest.

title: order the radii of isoelectronic ions by using nuclear charge with a fixed electron count, resisting the trends for neut (variant 3)
stem: Consider N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻ and Al³⁺, which all have 10 electrons. Which list gives them in order of decreasing radius, with the correct reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Al³⁺, because each has the same number of electrons, so the ion with the fewest protons holds them least tightly.
choices.rationale: Correct: All have 10 electrons; nuclear charges are +7, +8, +9 and +13, so radius decreases N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Al³⁺.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Al³⁺ > N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻, because aluminum is the heaviest atom of the four and has the most shells.
choices.rationale: Atomic mass is not the determining factor, and Al³⁺ has lost its n = 3 shell; with 13 protons holding 10 electrons it is the smallest ion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Al³⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻ > N³⁻, because more protons give a larger ion.
choices.rationale: More protons pull the electrons in more strongly, so Al³⁺ is the smallest and N³⁻ is the largest of the four.

choices.label: D
choices.text: O²⁻ > N³⁻ > F⁻ > Al³⁺, because the ion with the largest charge magnitude is largest only when it is an anion.
choices.rationale: N³⁻ has the largest charge magnitude among the anions, but within the series radius follows the proton count only, so N³⁻ with seven protons is the largest.

title: rank the lattice energies of ionic compounds by weighing both ion charges and ion sizes in Coulomb's law, rather than re
stem: Lattice energy is proportional to (q₁ × q₂)/d, where d is the distance between ion centers (the sum of the ionic radii). Ionic radii (pm): Li⁺ 76, Na⁺ 102, Mg²⁺ 72, Ca²⁺ 100, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181, O²⁻ 140, S²⁻ 184. Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing lattice energy (weakest first)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CaS < NaCl < MgO < LiF
choices.rationale: This ranks by interionic distance alone (284, 283, 212, 209 pm), ignoring that charges of 2+ and 2− give four times the attraction of 1+ and 1−.

choices.label: B
choices.text: LiF < NaCl < MgO < CaS
choices.rationale: This gets the charge groups right but puts the larger-ion compound as the stronger in each pair; for the same charges, the smaller distance gives the greater lattice energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NaCl < LiF < CaS < MgO

choices.label: D
choices.text: NaCl < LiF < MgO < CaS
choices.rationale: This orders the singly charged pair correctly, but in the doubly charged pair MgO (212 pm) has a smaller distance than CaS (284 pm), so MgO has the greater lattice energy.

title: rank the lattice energies of ionic compounds by weighing both ion charges and ion sizes in Coulomb's law, rather than re (variant 1)
stem: Lattice energy is proportional to (q₁ × q₂)/d, where d is the distance between ion centers (the sum of the ionic radii). Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, Sr²⁺ 118, Ba²⁺ 135, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181, O²⁻ 140. Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing lattice energy (weakest first)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: KCl < NaF < BaO < SrO

choices.label: B
choices.text: KCl < BaO < SrO < NaF
choices.rationale: This ranks by distance alone (319, 275, 258, 235 pm), ignoring that the 2+ and 2− charges of BaO and SrO give four times the attraction of the singly charged compounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NaF < KCl < SrO < BaO
choices.rationale: This reverses both pairs, treating a larger distance as a stronger attraction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: KCl < NaF < SrO < BaO
choices.rationale: This ranks the singly charged pair correctly but reverses the pair of oxides: SrO (258 pm) has a shorter distance than BaO (275 pm), so SrO has the greater lattice energy.

title: rank the lattice energies of ionic compounds by weighing both ion charges and ion sizes in Coulomb's law, rather than re (variant 2)
stem: Lattice energy is proportional to (q₁ × q₂)/d, where d is the distance between ion centers (the sum of the ionic radii). Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, Mg²⁺ 72, Ca²⁺ 100, Cl⁻ 181, F⁻ 133, O²⁻ 140. Which list shows the compounds NaCl, Na₂O, MgF₂ and CaO in order of increasing lattice energy (weakest first)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NaCl < Na₂O < CaO < MgF₂
choices.rationale: This ranks by distance alone (283, 242, 240, 205 pm), ignoring that the ions in CaO have charges 2+ and 2− while those in MgF₂ have 2+ and 1−.

choices.label: B
choices.text: NaCl < MgF₂ < Na₂O < CaO
choices.rationale: This orders Na₂O and MgF₂ wrongly; they have the same charge product (2), so the smaller distance in MgF₂ (205 pm versus 242 pm) gives the greater lattice energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NaCl < Na₂O < MgF₂ < CaO

choices.label: D
choices.text: Na₂O < NaCl < MgF₂ < CaO
choices.rationale: This ranks Na₂O below NaCl; Na₂O has a charge product of 2 compared with 1 for NaCl and a smaller distance, so it has the greater lattice energy.

title: rank the lattice energies of ionic compounds by weighing both ion charges and ion sizes in Coulomb's law, rather than re (variant 3)
stem: Lattice energy is proportional to (q₁ × q₂)/d, where d is the distance between ion centers (the sum of the ionic radii). Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, Mg²⁺ 72, Ca²⁺ 100, Rb⁺ 152, Cl⁻ 181, Br⁻ 196, S²⁻ 184, Se²⁻ 198. Which list shows the compounds RbBr, NaCl, CaSe and MgS in order of increasing lattice energy (weakest first)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RbBr < CaSe < NaCl < MgS
choices.rationale: This ranks by distance alone (348, 298, 283, 256 pm), ignoring that CaSe has charges of 2+ and 2− and so four times the charge product of NaCl.

choices.label: B
choices.text: RbBr < NaCl < CaSe < MgS

choices.label: C
choices.text: MgS < CaSe < NaCl < RbBr
choices.rationale: This reverses the whole order, treating a larger distance as giving a stronger attraction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: NaCl < RbBr < MgS < CaSe
choices.rationale: This wrongly places RbBr above NaCl and CaSe above MgS; for equal charges the smaller distance gives the larger lattice energy, so NaCl (283 pm) exceeds RbBr (348 pm).

title: combine electron transfer, ionic charges and formula ratios to count ions and transferred electrons in a sample.
stem: A sample of calcium nitride, Ca₃N₂, contains 6.02 × 10²² nitride ions, N³⁻. Which row correctly gives the number of Ca²⁺ ions in the sample and the total number of electrons transferred from calcium atoms to nitrogen atoms when the sample formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4.01 × 10²² Ca²⁺ ions; 8.03 × 10²² electrons.
choices.rationale: This inverts the ratio: the formula Ca₃N₂ has three Ca²⁺ for every two N³⁻, so there are 1.5 times as many Ca²⁺ ions as N³⁻ ions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 9.03 × 10²² Ca²⁺ ions; 9.03 × 10²² electrons.
choices.rationale: This counts only one electron per calcium ion; each Ca atom loses two electrons to become Ca²⁺.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 9.03 × 10²² Ca²⁺ ions; 2.71 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This gives each Ca atom three electrons, using the charge of the nitride ion; each Ca atom loses only two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 9.03 × 10²² Ca²⁺ ions; 1.81 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: Ca²⁺ = 6.02 × 10²² × 3/2 = 9.03 × 10²²; electrons = 2 × 9.03 × 10²² = 1.81 × 10²³ (equals 3 × 6.02 × 10²² gained by N).

title: combine electron transfer, ionic charges and formula ratios to count ions and transferred electrons in a sample. (variant 1)
stem: A sample of aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃, contains 1.204 × 10²³ Al³⁺ ions. Which row correctly gives the number of oxide ions, O²⁻, in the sample and the total number of electrons transferred from aluminum atoms to oxygen atoms when the sample formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 8.03 × 10²² O²⁻ ions; 1.61 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This inverts the ratio: Al₂O₃ has three O²⁻ for every two Al³⁺, so there are 1.5 times as many O²⁻ ions as Al³⁺ ions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.81 × 10²³ O²⁻ ions; 3.61 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: O²⁻ = 1.204 × 10²³ × 3/2 = 1.81 × 10²³; electrons = 3 × 1.204 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²³ (equals 2 × 1.81 × 10²³ gained by O).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1.81 × 10²³ O²⁻ ions; 1.81 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This counts one electron per oxide ion; each O atom gains two electrons to become O²⁻.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.81 × 10²³ O²⁻ ions; 2.41 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This gives each Al atom two electrons, using the charge of the oxide ion; each Al atom loses three.

title: combine electron transfer, ionic charges and formula ratios to count ions and transferred electrons in a sample. (variant 2)
stem: A sample of magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂, contains 1.505 × 10²⁴ ions in total (Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ together). Which row correctly gives the number of Mg²⁺ ions in the sample and the total number of electrons transferred from magnesium atoms to nitrogen atoms when the sample formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 7.53 × 10²³ Mg²⁺ ions; 1.51 × 10²⁴ electrons.
choices.rationale: This assumes half of the ions are Mg²⁺; the formula Mg₃N₂ has five ions per formula unit, three of them Mg²⁺.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 9.03 × 10²³ Mg²⁺ ions; 1.81 × 10²⁴ electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6.02 × 10²³ Mg²⁺ ions; 1.81 × 10²⁴ electrons.
choices.rationale: This uses 2/5 of the ions as Mg²⁺, which is the fraction of nitride ions; the Mg²⁺ ions make up 3/5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 9.03 × 10²³ Mg²⁺ ions; 9.03 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This counts only one electron per magnesium ion; each Mg atom loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺.

title: combine electron transfer, ionic charges and formula ratios to count ions and transferred electrons in a sample. (variant 3)
stem: A sample of lithium nitride, Li₃N, contains 3.61 × 10²³ lithium ions, Li⁺. Which row correctly gives the number of nitride ions, N³⁻, in the sample and the total number of electrons transferred from lithium atoms to nitrogen atoms when the sample formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1.08 × 10²⁴ N³⁻ ions; 3.61 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: This multiplies the number of Li⁺ ions by three; Li₃N has three Li⁺ for each N³⁻, so the N³⁻ count is one third of the Li⁺ count.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.20 × 10²³ N³⁻ ions; 1.08 × 10²⁴ electrons.
choices.rationale: This gives each Li atom three electrons, using the charge of the nitride ion; each Li atom loses only one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1.20 × 10²³ N³⁻ ions; 3.61 × 10²³ electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: N³⁻ = 3.61 × 10²³ ÷ 3 = 1.20 × 10²³; electrons = 1 × 3.61 × 10²³ (equals 3 × 1.20 × 10²³ gained by N).

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3.61 × 10²³ N³⁻ ions; 1.08 × 10²⁴ electrons.
choices.rationale: This assumes one N³⁻ per Li⁺, which does not balance the charge; Li₃N requires three Li⁺ to balance one N³⁻.
